How Nvidia’s Buyback Created Phantom Value
 
Plus, ‘existential risks to humanity’

Meanwhile, its rival OpenAI was about to release its most-capable model, but internal safety tests showed it could go rogue in scary ways. Speaking of scary, Treasury yields hit fresh multidecade highs Monday, weighing on stocks. Both have stabilized ahead of Tuesday’s open.

Deceptively large numbers?

 

Excitement about Nvidia’s blockbuster buyback announcement on Monday can be explained by the law of deceptively large numbers. We just made it up.

 

The “law of large numbers,” which lots of pundits get confused about, says that an increasingly large number of bets will eventually reflect the true odds. That’s why casinos don’t worry about going out of business after a few bad nights.

 

It’s often falsely taken to mean that a very big business can’t keep growing quickly, but there’s a grain of truth to that too. It might apply to Nvidia.

 

The chip maker’s $150 billion boost to its buyback authorization lighted a fire under its stock, tacking on $150 billion in market value Monday morning on a lousy day for tech stocks overall. Why, though?

 

When companies announce buybacks or dividends, investors often make the mental error of double counting. A dollar they own today as a shareholder is no more valuable when it moves to their bank account tomorrow.

 

Of course buybacks can be about more than money. They’re a sign of confidence that a company has more than enough cash to keep growing its business. They also mean management won’t be tempted to spend it on something dumb.

 

That’s a particular concern for Nvidia, which has backstopped customers to the tune of hundreds of billions of dollars. Ultimately, though, shareholders need to decide if they’re better off financially after a buyback. That isn’t a simple question. Boosting earnings per share is easy, but it isn’t enough.

 

Nvidia trades at a seemingly reasonable 25 times this fiscal year’s forecast earnings. Its operating margin has doubled in four years while sales grew 15-fold. Is that sustainable, and is its stock cheap enough for a buyback to create more wealth than a dividend?

 

Some 96% of analysts surveyed by FactSet think so, rating Nvidia a “buy” with an average target price 85% higher than today. But that brings us to that other law of large numbers. It’s hard to move the needle at a market value of $5.5 trillion, both in terms of a company getting bigger and rewarding shareholders.

 

Even Nvidia’s buyback, the largest in history, falls short of the percentage payout of many blue-chip companies.

 

That isn’t just Nvidia’s problem. Buybacks for the S&P 500 overall hit a record last year, topping $1 trillion, but less oomph as stock prices rose even faster. The index had one of its lowest buyback yields in recent history. It was more than twice as high back in 2018.

 

Nvidia, Apple, Meta and Alphabet topped the buyback list last year measured in dollars. But tech stocks overall had below-average buyback yields and also the lowest dividend yield of any sector.

 

Sometimes the numbers really do get too large.

Stocks I’m Watching

 

↘️ Lindt & Spruengli: Shares in the Swiss chocolate maker slid in Zurich after it cut its sales forecasts for the year, citing lower-than-expected orders in some European markets and blaming Europe’s summer heatwave.

 

↘️ Shein: The fast-fashion retailer’s stock tumbled in Hong Kong after its first earnings since listing disappointed. Tariffs and logistics costs helped knock Shein’s profit and stall its revenue growth.

 

↗️ Hapag-Lloyd: The German shipping company lifted its earnings forecast on strong market demand, boosting shares in Frankfurt.

 

🔎 Shell: British energy major said it would double production capacity at its LNG Canada facility as part of a bet on growing gas demand in Asia. Shell shares edged down premarket.
